Don’t buy a DIY regas kit or try to charge it yourself.

A fridge/freezer is a sealed refrigeration system: if it genuinely needs refrigerant, it has a leak or another fault that needs diagnosing and repairing first. Simply adding gas may work briefly at best, and can damage the compressor or make the repair harder.

Also, many modern domestic units use R600a (isobutane), which is highly flammable. Piercing a pipe, using the wrong refrigerant, overcharging, or introducing air/moisture is a real fire and equipment-damage risk. In the UK, work on many refrigerant systems is restricted to appropriately qualified engineers; even where R600a isn’t covered by the same F-gas rules, it is not a sensible DIY job.

What your symptoms could mean:
• refrigerant leak / loss of charge;
• failed or weak compressor;
• blockage in the sealed system;
• failed condenser or evaporator fan (if your model has one);
• defrost fault / ice blockage — though usually you’d see heavy frost;
• less commonly, a control or sensor issue.

A warm back/condenser and running compressor only show that it is trying to work — not that it is circulating refrigerant properly.

Safe checks you can do:
1. Check the temperature settings and make sure it hasn’t been put into an unusual mode.
2. Pull it away from the wall, vacuum dust from the rear/bottom vents or condenser area, and ensure good airflow around it.
3. Check whether any fan is running (often inside the freezer, and sometimes by the compressor). Don’t put fingers near moving parts.
4. Look for heavy frost/ice inside the freezer. If present, switch it off, empty it, leave doors open and defrost fully for 24–48 hours with towels down — don’t chip ice with tools or use heat.
5. Check door seals and that vents inside the freezer/fridge are not blocked.
6. If the compressor is repeatedly clicking on and off, is extremely hot, or you smell burning/chemical odours, unplug it and arrange repair.

If it has been running for several hours and both compartments are warm, book a refrigeration/appliance engineer or contact the manufacturer. Give them the model number and the refrigerant listed on the rating plate (often inside the fridge or at the rear). Ask for a diagnosis and quote before authorising a sealed-system repair; on an older appliance, compressor/leak repairs can cost enough that replacement is more economical.

Food-wise: move perishables to another fridge/cool box if possible. If refrigerated food has been above about 8°C for roughly 4 hours or more, be cautious and discard high-risk items such as meat, fish, dairy, cooked leftovers and opened chilled foods. Frozen food that still has ice crystals and has stayed cold may be salvageable; don’t rely on smell alone.
